title: The otters came back
teaches: Sea otters on the outer coast of Washington

blocks.text: In July 1969 a plane landed on the Olympic Peninsula carrying sea otters in crates, caught on Amchitka Island in the Aleutians. The United States was about to test nuclear bombs under Amchitka[^amchitka], and wildlife officers in Alaska were moving otters to coasts where they had been wiped out. Twenty-nine were released at Point Grenville, on the coast of the Quinault Indian Nation. The next summer thirty more were let go near La Push. Many of them died within weeks, of the stress of the journey or of fur fouled in the holding pens.

Sea otters had once lived along the whole of Washington's outer coast. From the 1740s Russian, then British and American, fur traders hunted them for the densest fur of any animal[^fur], and by about 1910 there were none left in Washington, and only a few small colonies anywhere. In 1977 a survey found nineteen otters on the Washington coast. For a while it seemed the release had failed.

It hadn't. The nineteen grew to about two hundred by 1989, and to more than two thousand by 2017, spread along the coast from around Destruction Island north to Cape Flattery and into the mouth of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Their numbers grew as lesson 2 predicts for a population with room: slowly at first, then faster, and lately more slowly again as the best stretches of coast fill up.

blocks.caption: The outer coast of Washington in twelve stretches, from Cape Flattery to Point Grenville. Otters grow in each stretch and wander to the next; where they settle, urchins thin and kelp grows. Dots on the chart are survey counts. A model.
blocks.task: Play the otters' return to the present

blocks.text: Lesson 8 told how James Estes found kelp forests around Aleutian islands with otters and bare urchin-covered rock around islands without them. The Washington coast ran the same experiment over time. Where the otters spread, they ate the urchins, and kelp beds grew where there had been urchin barrens. In 1989 David Duggins, Estes and a colleague compared Aleutian islands with and without otters, and found that mussels and barnacles near the kelp forests of otter islands grew several times faster, feeding on particles of kelp that drifted from the forest[^duggins].

The kelp forest is home to more than kelp. Young rockfish shelter in it, and so do the seals and seabirds that eat them. So the otters' return set off a chain that reached well beyond the urchins: in lesson 8's terms, a carnivore at the top made the coast greener, and the green fed many others.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: A sea otter has no blubber and keeps warm by burning food fast: it eats about a quarter of its weight a day. A 30-kilogram otter eats about 7 kilograms of urchins, crabs and clams a day, or roughly 2.5 tonnes a year. Two thousand otters eat about 5,000 tonnes of shellfish a year.

blocks.text: Otters eat urchins, but they also eat crabs, clams and abalone, the same shellfish that people harvest. In many places where otters have returned along the Pacific coast, shellfish harvests in the waters they settle have fallen. On Washington's coast the Makah, Quileute and Quinault peoples have harvested shellfish for thousands of years and hold treaty rights to them, and the return of the otter has brought both gains and losses to their fisheries[^treaty]. In southeast Alaska, where otters were also brought back, the commercial fisheries for Dungeness crab, the big crab of the Pacific Northwest, and for urchins, in some bays shrank sharply.

The story is a reminder that a cascade is a change, not simply an improvement. Before the fur trade, the Pacific coast had otters, kelp and fewer large shellfish; for a century without otters it had more shellfish and less kelp, and people built fisheries on that. Bringing a predator back restores an older balance, and someone usually pays for it.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the otters' return
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why were there no sea otters in Washington by about 1910?
choices: Fur traders had hunted them out
A disease spread through the colonies
items.why: From the 1740s otters were hunted for their dense fur across the North Pacific.

items.ask: Where did Washington's otters come from in 1969 and 1970?
choices: Colonies on the British Columbia coast
An aquarium breeding programme in California
items.why: Fifty-nine were flown from Amchitka, ahead of nuclear tests there, and released at Point Grenville and La Push.

items.ask: Only nineteen otters were counted in 1977. What happened next?
choices: They grew to about two thousand by 2017
items.why: A small population with room to grow grows slowly at first, then faster.

items.ask: Why did kelp beds grow where the otters spread?
choices: Otters ate the urchins that graze kelp
Otters planted kelp by dragging it
Otters ate the fish that eat kelp
items.why: Lesson 8's cascade: otters down, urchins up, kelp gone; otters back, urchins down, kelp back.

choices: People who harvest crabs, clams and urchins
The fish that shelter in kelp
items.why: Otters eat the same shellfish people harvest, so shellfish catches fall where otters settle.

summary: **Fur traders wiped out Washington's sea otters by about 1910.** They had the densest fur of any animal.
**Fifty-nine otters were brought from Amchitka in 1969 and 1970.** Only nineteen were counted in 1977.
**They grew to over two thousand by 2017.** Slowly at first, then faster, as lesson 2 predicts.
**Kelp grew back where they settled.** Otters ate the urchins, lesson 8's cascade on Washington's coast.
**An otter eats about a quarter of its weight a day.** Two thousand otters eat thousands of tonnes of shellfish a year.
**Shellfish harvesters often lose.** Bringing a predator back restores an older balance, and someone pays for it.

duggins.title: Kelp on the menu
duggins.text: Duggins and colleagues traced the carbon of kelp, which has its own chemical signature, into mussels, barnacles and fish, showing that much of the food of animals near a kelp forest starts as kelp.

treaty.title: The treaties
treaty.text: The treaties of the 1850s between the United States and the tribes of western Washington kept the tribes' right to fish and gather shellfish at their usual places. The Makah, whose land is at Cape Flattery, also kept the right to hunt whales.

fur.title: The densest fur
fur.text: A sea otter has up to about a million hairs in a square centimetre of skin, more than any other animal. Air trapped in the fur keeps the cold water off its skin, which is why oil, which mats the fur, is so deadly to otters.

amchitka.title: Amchitka
amchitka.text: The United States set off three underground nuclear tests on Amchitka between 1965 and 1971. Protests against the last and largest, Cannikin, led a group in Vancouver to charter a boat to sail to the island, and the group became Greenpeace.
